body:
Religious Reform in Nineteenth-Century India

The nineteenth century witnessed important changes in Indian religious and social life. British colonial rule, Western education, Christian missionary activity and the expansion of printing encouraged debates about religious beliefs, social customs and the condition of Indian society.

Indian thinkers responded in different ways. Some challenged practices such as caste discrimination and restrictions on women. Others sought to revive religious traditions or reinterpret them for changing circumstances. These approaches were not necessarily opposed: a reformer could draw upon ancient religious ideas while advocating changes in contemporary society.

The tradition associated with Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa and Swami Vivekananda developed primarily around spiritual experience, harmony among religions and the application of religious principles to human welfare.

Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa (1836–1886)

Sri Ramakrishna was born on 18 February 1836 at Kamarpukur in Bengal. His childhood name was Gadadhar Chattopadhyay. He became closely associated with the Dakshineswar Kali Temple near Calcutta, where he pursued an intense spiritual life.

Unlike reformers who concentrated on establishing schools, writing social legislation or forming political associations, Ramakrishna primarily taught through spiritual practice, conversations and personal example. His teachings attracted householders, intellectuals and young disciples.

Religious Experience and Different Paths to God

Ramakrishna's central teaching was that sincere spiritual practice could lead people towards the ultimate divine reality through different religious paths. He practised forms of Hindu devotion and non-dualistic meditation and also undertook disciplines associated with Islam and Christianity.

His understanding of religious harmony did not require every religion to have identical rituals, scriptures or doctrines. Rather, he maintained that differences in religious practice need not prevent genuine spiritual realization.

Religious universalism

In the Ramakrishna tradition, religious universalism means recognizing the spiritual value of different religious paths instead of treating one community's form of worship as the only possible path to divine realization.

This approach was significant in a period when missionary criticism, religious controversy and competing claims about the superiority of particular traditions were prominent in public debate.

Devotion, Vedanta and Spiritual Realization

Ramakrishna's teachings drew upon several streams of Hindu religious thought. Bhakti emphasizes devotion to God, while Advaita Vedanta teaches the fundamental non-duality of ultimate reality.

Ramakrishna valued devotional worship as well as non-dualistic spiritual experience. His approach encouraged followers to look beyond differences in particular forms of worship and recognize the deeper spiritual purpose of religious life.

From Spiritual Teacher to Reform Tradition

One of Ramakrishna's most influential disciples was Narendranath Datta, who later became Swami Vivekananda. Vivekananda carried his teacher's emphasis on spiritual unity into a wider programme of religious education, social service and international engagement.

Ramakrishna died on 16 August 1886. After his death, his young disciples established a monastic brotherhood that became the foundation of the Ramakrishna Order.

Sri Sarada Devi (1853–1920), Ramakrishna's spiritual consort, subsequently became an important spiritual guide to this community. She is revered within the tradition as the Holy Mother.

Ramakrishna was the spiritual teacher whose life inspired the movement. The organized Ramakrishna Mission was founded later by Swami Vivekananda. Their roles should not be confused.

Prelims focus

  • Sri Ramakrishna: 1836–1886.
  • Birthplace: Kamarpukur, Bengal.
  • Childhood name: Gadadhar Chattopadhyay.
  • Principal religious association: Dakshineswar Kali Temple, near Calcutta.
  • Chief disciple: Swami Vivekananda, originally Narendranath Datta.
  • Central teaching: spiritual harmony and the possibility of realization through different religious paths.
  • Trap: Ramakrishna inspired the movement, but Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed p. 106; Belur Math, Sri Ramakrishna, sections Childhood, Following Other Faiths and Last Days; Belur Math, Sri Sarada Devi, biographical account; Belur Math, Ideology, section Harmony of Religions. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]

body:
From Narendranath Datta to Swami Vivekananda

Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902) was born as Narendranath Datta in Calcutta on 12 January 1863. He became a disciple of Sri Ramakrishna and later emerged as one of the most influential interpreters of Vedanta in modern India.

Following Ramakrishna's death in 1886, Vivekananda participated in establishing a monastic brotherhood. During his travels across India, particularly from 1890 to 1893, he encountered widespread poverty, inadequate education and social inequality.

These experiences strengthened his conviction that spiritual development and national improvement required the uplift of ordinary people, not merely philosophical discussion among educated groups.

What Is Neo-Vedanta?

Vedanta refers to philosophical traditions drawing especially upon the Upanishads and other foundational Hindu texts. Among its important schools, Advaita Vedanta teaches the non-duality of ultimate reality.

Neo-Vedanta is a term used for modern reinterpretations of Vedantic thought that emphasize its wider human relevance, spiritual universality and application to contemporary life. Swami Vivekananda is one of its principal representatives.

Vivekananda did not establish Vedanta as a new philosophy. He presented existing Vedantic ideas in a form that addressed the religious, social and intellectual concerns of the modern world.

His teaching emphasized the potential divinity of every human being. From this understanding followed the ethical importance of dignity, self-confidence and service to others.

Practical Vedanta

Practical Vedanta means applying Vedantic principles to everyday conduct. If the same spiritual reality is present in all beings, serving people in need becomes a meaningful expression of spiritual life rather than an activity separate from religion.

The Four Yogas

Vivekananda emphasized that people could develop spiritually through different but complementary disciplines. His presentation commonly distinguishes 4 yogas.

  • Jnana Yoga: The path of knowledge, inquiry and discrimination between the ultimate reality and appearances.
  • Bhakti Yoga: The path of devotion and love directed towards God.
  • Karma Yoga: The path of selfless action, performed without selfish attachment to its results.
  • Raja Yoga: The path emphasizing mental discipline, concentration and meditation.

These paths were not presented as mutually exclusive religious organizations. Their combination allowed individuals with different inclinations to pursue spiritual development.

The World's Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 1893

A decisive event in Vivekananda's public career was his participation in the World's Parliament of Religions, held in Chicago, United States, in September 1893, in connection with the World's Columbian Exposition.

On 11 September 1893, Vivekananda delivered his famous opening address, beginning with the words Sisters and Brothers of America.

He presented Hindu religious thought to an international audience and argued for religious tolerance and acceptance. His message opposed fanaticism and emphasized that religious differences should not become grounds for hostility.

The address helped make Vivekananda an internationally recognized interpreter of Hindu philosophy. His subsequent lectures and writings contributed to the spread of Vedanta and yoga in Western intellectual and religious circles.

Religious tolerance means allowing people to follow different beliefs. Vivekananda's language of acceptance went further by recognizing spiritual value in different religious traditions. This did not mean that all religions possessed identical teachings or practices.

Vivekananda and Indian Nationalism

Vivekananda linked India's regeneration with education, the dignity of labour, social service and renewed confidence in Indian intellectual and spiritual traditions.

His speeches challenged feelings of cultural inferiority that colonial rule could encourage. He emphasized that a strong society required physically, intellectually and morally capable citizens.

His influence on nationalism was therefore primarily cultural, moral and intellectual. He was not the founder of the Indian National Congress, nor did his spiritual message amount to a programme of electoral politics.

At the same time, his outlook was international rather than narrowly nationalist. He advocated respect among religions and cooperation among the peoples of the world.

Prelims focus

  • Swami Vivekananda: 1863–1902; original name Narendranath Datta.
  • Guru: Sri Ramakrishna Paramahamsa.
  • World's Parliament of Religions: Chicago, 1893.
  • Opening address: 11 September 1893.
  • Principal philosophical association: Neo-Vedanta and Practical Vedanta.
  • Four yogas: Jnana, Bhakti, Karma and Raja.
  • Trap: Vivekananda popularized Vedanta internationally; he did not originate the ancient Vedantic philosophical tradition.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, printed p. 106; Belur Math, Swami Vivekananda, sections Discovery of Real India, World Parliament of Religions and Founding of Ramakrishna Mission; Belur Math, Ideology, sections Practical Vedanta and Service; Ramakrishna-Vivekananda Center of New York, Addresses at the Parliament of Religions, Response to Welcome, 11 September 1893; Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, September 11, 1893. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The 4 yogas in Vivekananda's presentation of spiritual development.

title: Swami Vivekananda: Neo-Vedanta, Practical Religion and Global Religious Engagement

body:
Formation of the Ramakrishna Order

After Sri Ramakrishna's death in 1886, his young disciples formed a monastic brotherhood at Baranagar near Calcutta. Swami Vivekananda became its principal organizing figure.

This monastic community developed into the Ramakrishna Math. Its members combined spiritual discipline, study, meditation and teaching with an increasing concern for human welfare.

The organized service movement took a more definite form after Vivekananda returned from his travels abroad.

Foundation of the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897

Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission on 1 May 1897 at a gathering in Calcutta.

The organization was established to put the spiritual principles associated with Sri Ramakrishna into practice through education, religious instruction and humanitarian service.

The Mission brought together monks and lay supporters. Its activities developed to include schools, hospitals, medical assistance, relief work and programmes for the welfare of disadvantaged communities.

The Ramakrishna Mission was founded in 1897 by Swami Vivekananda. The earlier monastic brotherhood arose after Ramakrishna's death in 1886. These are related but distinct historical developments.

Ramakrishna Math and Ramakrishna Mission: The Distinction

The Math and Mission are closely connected institutions inspired by the same spiritual ideals. However, they are legally and financially distinct organizations.

  • Ramakrishna Math: Primarily the monastic organization concerned with spiritual discipline, religious teaching and the life of the Ramakrishna Order.
  • Ramakrishna Mission: The organization through which monks and lay members undertake coordinated educational, charitable, medical and relief activities.

Their shared headquarters are at Belur Math in Howrah, West Bengal, on the western bank of the Hooghly River near Kolkata.

Vivekananda acquired land at Belur in 1898 for a permanent monastery. Thus, the year 1898 is associated with the development of Belur Math, not the original founding of the Mission.

Service as a Spiritual Duty

The central principle of the movement is that service to human beings can be understood as service to God. The poor, sick and disadvantaged are not merely recipients of charity; they possess the same inherent spiritual dignity as others.

This is an application of Practical Vedanta. The belief in the divinity present in human beings creates a moral responsibility to act for their welfare.

The guiding motto is Atmano mokshartham jagat hitaya cha, meaning for one's own spiritual liberation and for the welfare of the world.

The motto combines 2 purposes: spiritual progress of the individual and practical service to society.

Relationship with Indian Nationalism

The Ramakrishna-Vivekananda tradition contributed to the growth of Indian self-confidence by emphasizing India's philosophical heritage and the need to uplift the masses.

Its social message encouraged education, self-reliance, service and concern for marginalized people. These ideas influenced the broader atmosphere of national awakening.

However, the Ramakrishna Mission is a non-political spiritual and humanitarian organization. Its cultural influence on nationalism should not be confused with direct participation as a political party or nationalist association.

The Gujarat Connection

Swami Vivekananda travelled extensively through Gujarat and Kathiawar during 1891–1892, before his journey to Chicago.

Places associated with his travels include Ahmedabad, Limbdi, Junagadh, Porbandar, Dwarka and Baroda.

He spent time in Porbandar, where he interacted with scholars and administrators. These contacts formed part of the intellectual and spiritual preparation for his later international work.

The tradition subsequently acquired a permanent institutional presence in Saurashtra. Shri Ramakrishna Ashrama at Rajkot was established in 1927.

These connections demonstrate that Vivekananda's travels and influence extended well beyond Bengal before and after his international recognition.

Prelims focus

  • 1886: Ramakrishna's death and the subsequent formation of the Baranagar monastic brotherhood.
  • 1 May 1897: Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission.
  • 1898: Land acquired at Belur for a permanent monastery.
  • Belur Math: Howrah, West Bengal.
  • 1891–1892: Vivekananda travelled through Gujarat and Kathiawar.
  • 1927: Establishment of Shri Ramakrishna Ashrama, Rajkot.
  • Trap: The Mission's influence on national awakening does not make it a political organization.

[Sources: Belur Math, About Us, sections Motto, Ideals and Headquarters; Belur Math, Swami Vivekananda, sections Beginnings of a Monastic Brotherhood, Founding of Ramakrishna Mission and Belur Math; Belur Math, Frequently Asked Questions, What Is the Ramakrishna Order?; Shri Ramakrishna Ashrama Rajkot, History of the Ashrama, section Swami Vivekananda in Gujarat; Belur Math, Ramakrishna Math Rajkot, historical introduction. Websites consulted 20 November 2026.]
